list.listitem: Acromegaly carries significant risk of morbidity/mortality and a high index of suspicion should be maintained when considering biochemical screening. C

Serum IGF-1 level is the best initial biochemical test. If elevated (for age/sex), failure to suppress growth hormone (GH) levels less than 1 ng/mL following a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test confirms the diagnosis. C
First-line treatment is surgical removal of the adenoma, which should only be undertaken at experienced surgical centers. C

Somatostatin receptor ligands are first-line medical therapy, followed by dopamine agonists or GH-receptor antagonists. These agents may be helpful in increasing surgical cure rates when given preoperatively. B
Radiotherapy is an option if surgical and medical therapies are ineffective or incompletely effective. B
The goal of treatment is to eliminate adenoma mass effect and achieve biochemical control; identification and management of co-morbidities is crucial to quality of life and prolonging health. B

background.definition: Acromegaly is a clinical condition that results from excess secretion of GH.

list.listitem: The annual incidence is 3 to 4 cases per million people.
Authors of a review of population studies found annual incidence rates ranging from 0.2 to 1.1 cases per 100,000.
Prevalence ranges between 2.8 and 13.7 cases per 100,000 people, with the disease diagnosed most often in the 5th decade after a delay in diagnosis of 4.5 to 5 years.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 22 studies found a pooled global prevalence of 5.9 (95% CI 4.4-7.9) per 100,000 persons, although between-study heterogeneity was high.
Mortality rates for patients with acromegaly are 1.6 to 3 times greater than that of the general population, predominantly from cardiovascular and respiratory disease.
Rates of hypertension among patients with active acromegaly range from 30% to 60% in case series.
Diabetes is present in 12% to 56% of patients with acromegaly due to a combination of insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia and increased gluconeogenesis from GH and IGF-1 excess.

Although changes in thyroid function, including hyperthyroidism (5%-14.7%), thyroid nodules (39%-65%), and goiter (up to 92%), occur in patients with acromegaly, these often normalize following treatment. Thyroid cancer occurs in higher numbers of patients compared to controls (3.2% vs. 0.3%) based on an analysis of available studies.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 41 studies found that patients with acromegaly had a high frequency of vertebral fractures (odds ratio, 8.26; 95% CI, 2.91-23.39) associated with male gender, hypogonadism, and active acromegaly.

About half of patients with acromegaly have hypogonadism resulting from tumor mass effect, and/ or concomitant hyperprolactinemia. Hypogonadism may compromise sexual function, fertility, body composition, well-being, and bone health.

Sleep apnea is present in 20% to 80% of patients with acromegaly; most (2/3rds) of cases are obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) due to anatomical changes including soft tissue swelling and one third are central sleep apnea from impaired brain control of respiration due to excess GH and IGF-1. Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies found similar rates of OSA between patients with active and inactive disease.

Quality of life, often measured using the Acromegaly Quality of Life Questionnaire, is often poorly reported in studies of patients with acromegaly; even when reported, authors of a meta-analysis found discrepancies between patient reported outcomes and biochemical measures in about one third, with most showing lack of improvement in quality of life and symptoms despite improved biochemical outcomes.
Greater than 95% of cases are caused by a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. About 80% of these tumors are considered large when discovered, likely due to delay in diagnosis of up to 10 years.
Rarer causes include secretion of GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) by tumors of the hypothalamus and ectopic GHRH or GH secretion by neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine tumors.
Excess GH stimulates IGF-1 production from the liver.
Elevated levels of GH and IGF-1 account for the signs and symptoms of acromegaly (see section on Using the History and Physical under Diagnosis).

Higher levels of sclerostin found in patients with active acromegaly compared to healthy controls may contribute to increased fracture risk. In one study, there was a moderate positive correlation between sclerostin and IGF-1 levels (rho = 0.54) and between sclerostin and GH levels (rho = 0.41).
Clinical diagnosis of acromegaly is often delayed due to the slow progression of signs and symptoms (eg, headache, lateral visual field deficit, enlarged jaws, hands and feet, and macroglossia). C

Serum IGF-1 level is the best initial biochemical test. If elevated for age and sex, failure to suppress GH levels less than 1 ng/mL following a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test confirms the diagnosis. C
Once biochemically confirmed, order contrast MRI with multiplanar thin sellar imaging of the pituitary. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Clinical features of acromegaly in the absence of elevated biochemical markers
Rare hereditary disorder with hypertrophic skin changes, periosteal bone formation, finger clubbing

list.listitem: The direct mass effect of the pituitary adenoma can cause headaches and lateral visual field cuts from compression of the optic chiasm. Herniation of cerebellar tonsils can also occur, contributing to the neurologic findings.
Neurocognitive changes such as memory difficulty can occur and appear associated with duration of untreated acromegaly. Memory deficits may not reverse following curative surgery.

Acral and soft tissue overgrowth results in an enlarged jaw, enlarged hands and feet, coarsened facial features, increased separation between teeth, macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea. Hyperhidrosis is another common manifestation of acromegaly.
Growth of articular cartilage and periarticular ligaments results in significant arthropathy in more than half of patients.
Impaired glucose tolerance is seen in 16% to 46% and type 2 diabetes mellitus occurs in 19% to 56%.

Based on a Mexican nationwide registry of 2057 patients with acromegaly diagnosed after 1990, hypertension, glucose intolerance, diabetes, and dyslipidemia were present in 27%, 18.4%, 30%, and 24% of the patients, respectively.
The direct effect of IGF-1 on myocardial tissues results in cardiac hypertrophy in greater than 90% of long-term patients, leading to early diastolic and late systolic dysfunction.
Mentrual irregularities can occur in women and sexual dysfunction in men with acromegaly.

Clinicians should consider the diagnosis of acromegaly in patients with two or more of the following: new onset diabetes, diffuse arthralgias, new onset or difficult-to-control hypertension, cardiac disease, fatigue, headaches, carpal tunnel syndrome, sleep apnea, diaphoresis, loss of vision, colon polyps, and progressive jaw malocclusion.

Symptoms can be measured using the Patient Assessed Acromegaly Symptom Questionnaire – a disease-specific, self-rating questionnaire consisting of 5 items assessing soft-tissue swelling, arthralgia, headache, excessive perspiration, and fatigue.
IGF-1 is the best initial biochemical test if acromegaly is clinically suspected.

If patients have an elevated serum IGF-1 value for age and sex, a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test is performed. GH levels are sampled every 30 minutes for 2 hours. Acromegaly is confirmed if all GH values are greater than 1 ng/mL. Under normal conditions, GH levels are suppressed following a glucose load.

Some patients have a paradoxical response of GH to an oral glucose load, defined as a 30% increase in the serum GH level after the OG load relative to the pretest basal GH level. Investigators in one study found 30% of 63 patients were paradoxical responders and these patients demonstrated more acral and soft-tissue overgrowth and greater GH suppression following treatment with octreotide or bromocriptine than non-paradoxical responders.

In a larger study of 496 patients with acromegaly, 184 (37%) were paradoxical responders. These patients also showed a higher remission rate in response to somatostatin analogues (52% vs. 26% in non-paradoxical responders) and a more marked drop in IGF-1 and GH after 6 months of therapy. Paradoxical responders were, on average 4 years older and had smaller, less invasive tumors.

Once GH hypersecretion is confirmed, a contrast MRI with multiplanar thin sellar imaging of the pituitary should be obtained to confirm the presence of a pituitary adenoma. If MRI is contraindicated or unavailable, consider performing a computed tomography (CT) scan (AACE).
If optic chiasmal compression is noted on MRI, visual field testing should be performed (AACE).
If there is no pituitary adenoma, a GHRH level should be obtained; if elevated, this suggests hypothalamic hypersecretion or ectopic secretion.

If MRI does not reveal a pituitary tumor, a search for an ectopic source should be undertaken with studies such as a chest CT scan and Octreoscan (scintigraphy using radiolabeled octreotide) to find a carcinoid or other tumor (AACE).

Solid organ stiffness as measured by elastography was found to be increased among patients with active acromegaly compared to treated patients or controls and may be useful as an additional measure of active disease.

Signs and symptoms consistent with acromegaly should prompt biochemical screening with IGF-1, followed by confirmatory testing by GH measurement after an oral glucose load. GH reflects tumor secretory activity and IGF-I levels reflect peripheral disease activity.
Once the biochemical diagnosis has been made, an MRI of the pituitary should be obtained to confirm the presence of a pituitary adenoma.
If there is no pituitary adenoma, GHRH should be obtained to evaluate for hypothalamic hypersecretion or ectopic secretion.

Additional testing in patients with acromegaly includes assessment for hypertension, diabetes, osteoarthritis, sleep apnea, and cardiac disease including risk factors (eg, lipid levels); for the latter, consider an electrocardiogram and echocardiogram.

The Acromegaly Consensus Group (2020) recommend obtaining a baseline electrocardiogram and echocardiogram, fasting blood sugar every 6 months during active disease or somatostatin receptor ligand treatment, serum free T4 annually, dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry every 2 years, and assessing for sleep apnea at baseline and prior to surgery with the Epworth Sleepiness Scale or a sleep study if sleep apnea is suspected.
Additional laboratory tests include serum prolactin (possible hyperprolactinemia) and assessment of pituitary function (for potential hypopituitarism). See follow-up section below.

Screening for colon cancer is also suggested with colonoscopy at diagnosis. The Acromegaly Consensus Group (2020) recommend colonoscopy every 10 years or more frequently if IGF-1 remains persistently elevated or if the patient has an abnormal colonoscopy or family history of colon cancer. However, they acknowledge that cancer-specific mortality rates for patients with acromegaly are similar to those observed in the general population.
If thyroid nodularity is present, consider thyroid ultrasound.
All patients should be treated (even if they are asymptomatic or there is no evidence of progression) unless they are not expected to live long enough to benefit from therapy. B

The goals of treatment are to eliminate adenoma mass effect and achieve biochemical control, reduce disease signs and symptoms, improve quality of life, prevent early mortality, and prevent or reduce medical co-morbidities. C
Surgery is treatment of choice; if patients are not surgical candidates or refuse surgery, consider medical treatment. C

First-line medical treatment is with somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs). If these are ineffective or not tolerated, dopamine agonists or GH receptor antagonists may be considered alone or in combination with somatostatin analog therapy (SSAs). B
If biochemical control cannot be achieved with surgery and medication, consider radiotherapy with concurrent medical therapy to bridge the latency period of effectiveness. B

Medical therapy should be considered the first-line treatment in patients who refuse surgery or who are unsuitable surgical candidates due to medically unstable conditions or anesthesia risk. Treatment with pharmacologic agents may reverse the effects of acromegaly and allow these patients to become future surgical candidates.

The use of primary medical therapy in patients unlikely to be cured by surgery can be considered but is controversial. Medical therapy is recommended for patients with persistent disease following surgery.

Subcutaneous SRLs, octreotide, pasireotide, or lanreotide, bind somatostatin receptors to inhibit GH secretion and are first-line agents for the medical treatment of acromegaly. These agents can reduce GH and IGF-1 levels and tumor size. An additional benefit of these two medications is a generally neutral effect on glucose control, particularly important in those with concomitant diabetes.

Authors of a meta-analysis of participant data from 2 cohort studies with 622 patients found that lower baseline IGF-1 concentration and lower bodyweight were associated with biochemical response to first-generation SRLs.
In an RCT of 30 patients with acromegaly partially responsive to SRLs, use of either high dose or high frequency lanreotide Autogel resulted in normalization of IGF-1 values in 27.6% of patients.

For patients preferring oral therapy, one RCT of 56 patients demonstrated that switching from an injectable SRL to oral octreotide resulted in maintenance of normalization of IGF-1 levels in 58.2% vs. 19.4% of those switched to placebo. Median time to loss of IGF-1 response for patients receiving placebo was 16 weeks.

Pasireotide is a novel somatostatin receptor ligand that can also be used to control hormonal hypersecretion. Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 studies found overall tumor shrinkage in 37.7% (95%CI 18.7% - 61.5%) of patients with acromegaly; high study heterogeneity was noted (I2 90%).

An RCT compared long-acting release (LAR) pasireotide 40 mg every 28 days with LAR octreotide 20 mg every 28 days in 358 newly diagnosed patients with acromegaly. The dose could be titrated upward to 60 mg and 30 mg respectively if GH levels remained elevated. At 12 months, biochemical control was more common with pasireotide (31% vs. 19%, NNT = 8), but hyperglycemia was more common in those given pasireotide (57% vs. 22% NNH = 3).

In patients with only modest elevations of serum IGF-1 and mild signs and symptoms of GH excess, a trial of a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline is suggested by the Endocrine Society guidelines as initial adjuvant medical therapy. Oral dopamine agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine) are used in patients who do not tolerate SRLs, or, less frequently, in combination with SRLs.

Pegvisomant is a subcutaneous GH receptor antagonist that decreases IGF-1 levels. Its role in therapy is still being determined, but is most often used in combination with SSAs in patients with an inadequate response to those agents. Pegvisomant does not inhibit GH secretion or induce a decrease in adenoma size. Therefore, it should be used with caution in an aggressive tumor mass causing compressive symptoms. Side effects of pegvisomant include flu-like illness, allergic reactions, increased liver enzymes, and tumor enlargement.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies of pegvisomant alone and 5 in combination with other agents found improvements in glucose metabolism in both groups with use of this agent.

In a longitudinal retrospective international study of 55 patients with acromegaly resistant to first-generation SRL, use of pasireotide but not pegvisomant reduced incident vertebral fractures (25% vs. 77.8%) despite a similar proportion of patients achieving biochemical control (66.7% in each group).

The AACE guideline recommends use of combination SRL and a dopamine agonist in patients who do not achieve control with an SRL alone. In one systematic review and meta-analysis of patients with acromegaly, about one third receiving carbergoline alone achieved normal IGF-1 levels and half normalized IGF-1 when cabergoline was added to ongoing SRL treatment that had failed to normalize IGF-1. Side effects of dopamine agonists include gastrointestinal upset, orthostatic hypotension, headache and nasal congestion.

For patients with no biochemical response to SRL/dopamine agonist combination, a GH receptor antagonist should be tried. If there is a partial biochemical response, AACE recommends combination SRL/GH antagonist.
Combination pegvisomant and cabergoline use has been reported and may provide better control in some patients.

In a small 3-arm trial using a combination of two SRLs plus pegvisomant, investigators found low-dose SRL (lanreotide 60 mg/octreotide LAR 10 mg) plus weekly pegvisomant (40-160 mg/week) was as effective (22/23) as the other strategies with respect to IGF-1 control and least costly (mean, $9837 ± 1375 per month); approximately 30% of patients required pegvisomant dose up titration and rates of adverse events were <10%.

In a case series of 6 patients who were resistant to SRLs and had large, invasive tumors with low somatostatin receptor subtype 2 expression, combination treatment with pasireotide and pegvisomant was successful in controlling the disease.

The Endocrine Society Clinical guidelines recommend against routine use of preoperative medical therapy to improve biochemical control after surgery. Preoperative treatment with SRLs, which are somatostatin receptor subtype specific analogues, should be considered for patients with severe pharyngeal thickness and sleep apnea or high out-put heart failure

Preoperative treatment with octreotide may be of short-term benefit to patients with invasive macroadenomas. Octreotide is under testing as a subcutaneous implant; early testing looks promising for stable drug release and being well tolerated. Side effects of octreotide include gastrointestinal upset, malabsorption, constipation, gallbladder disease, hair loss, and bradycardia.

In an RCT of 49 patients with newly diagnosed acromegaly from invasive pituitary macroadenoma, 3-month lanreotide treatment prior to transsphenoidal surgery resulted in higher cure rates (11 of 24 vs. 5 of 25 patients, respectively). An earlier RCT of 108 patients with macroadenomas causing acromegaly also found pretreatment with lanreatide for 4 months increased cure rates (24 of 29 pretreated patients vs. 9 of 49 direct surgical patients).

GH deficiency can occur in as many as 50% of treated patients with acromegaly. One 6-month RCT of 20 subjects with prior acromegaly and current GH deficiency demonstrated that those randomized to GH replacement had a reduction of visceral adipose tissue, increased fat-free mass, decreased C-reactive protein, and reported improved quality of life. There were no differences in other cardiac risk factors or glycosylated hemoglobin. A second RCT of 42 patients also found improved body composition and quality of life in addition to improved lipid profiles in patients treated with GH.

Transsphenoidal surgical treatment is considered the first therapeutic option in most patients with acromegaly. Neurosurgery is immediately effective in debulking tumor and reducing pressure on optic tracts.
In the best centers, surgical remission rates are 80% for microadenomas (<1 cm) and 50% for macroadenomas (>1 cm).
In inexperienced centers, complication rates are 3- to 4-fold higher than at experienced centers.

In a single-institute retrospective analysis of 81 patients with GH-secreting adenomas undergoing transsphenoidal procedures from 2000 to 2016, biochemical remission at 1-year post surgery was achieved in 59 cases (73%). However, only 41 patients (51%) remained in primary surgical remission (without any adjuvant treatment) at their last follow-up appointment (mean 100 ± 61 months) - a recurrence rate of 31% (18 of 59 patients).

In a case series of patients undergoing endonasal endoscopic surgery for acromegaly due to GH-secreting adenomas, there was no significant difference in overall disease control rates between the 33 patients undergoing first-time surgery and the 11 patients undergoing reoperation (71.4% and 63.6%, respectively). In their meta-analysis of 29 papers using this type of surgery, overall rates of disease control were 56.4% (95% CI, 49%-63%) for 2189 first-time operations vs. 46.8% (95% CI, 20%-74%) for 161 reoperations.

Patients who continue to have GH hypersecretion after surgical treatment are candidates for pituitary irradiation, provided the distance between the residual tumor and the optic nerve is >5 mm. The Endocrine Society guidelines suggest use of stereotactic radiotherapy (SRS) as the preferred method for patients with residual tumor mass following surgery, and if medical therapy is unavailable, unsuccessful, or not tolerated.

In a systematic review of SRS as adjuvant radiation-based therapy for patients with acromegaly and pituitary adenomas, about half had disease control without medication and an additional quarter were controlled with medication. In a more recent meta-analysis of single institution outcomes for SRS, for patients with acromegaly, random effects estimates for crude tumor control rate, crude endocrine remission rate, and any new hypopituitarism rates were 97.0% (95% CI 96.0%-98.0%), 44.0% (95% CI 35.0%-53.0%), and 17.0% (95% CI 13.0%-23.0%), respectively.
In a multicenter study of 26 patients with medically-refractory acromegaly who received primary SRS, actuarial endocrine remission rates at 2 and 5 years were 20% and 42%, respectively.
Results of upfront Gamma Knife radiosurgery were reported for 46 patients of whom 25 had acromegaly. Remission was seen in only 28% of patients with acromegaly vs. 81% with Cushing’s disease.
GH and IGF-1 levels decline over several years after irradiation; therefore, medical therapy is required to bridge the latency period.
Hypopituitarism is a common side effect in patients treated with radiation.

In an RCT including 60 patients with acromegaly, participation in an 8-week face-to-face mindfulness training program vs. a control group resulted in lower pain scores, increased nighttime hours in bed and improvement in self-compassion.
All patients suspected of having acromegaly should be referred to an endocrinologist.
If patients have evidence of increased intracranial pressure or rapidly progressive visual field defects, urgent neurosurgical evaluation is required.

Mortality rates for patients with acromegaly are 1.6 to 3 times greater than that of the general population, predominantly from cardiovascular and respiratory disease. A In a Korean cohort study of 718 patients with acromegaly, mortality risk was significant higher in women (HR 1.75; 95% CI, 1.07-2.84).

Therapy that achieves biochemical goals has traditionally been believed to reduce mortality rates to that of the general population. A recent meta-analysis, however, suggests that even with biochemical control mortality rates may be increased, possibly due to irreversible effects of prior excess IGF-1 exposure. B
In one case series with a mean follow-up of 3.8 years, postoperative GH levels at 24 hours was a very good predictor of long-term remission in acromegaly.

Cavernous sinus invasion is a significant, independent predictor of unfavorable outcome. Despite this, one study of 150 consecutive patients undergoing primary transsphenoidal surgery for acromegaly, reported remission in 69.1% (38 of 55) of patients with invasion compared to 84.7% (127 of 150) of those without invasion.

Based on a systematic review of 35 studies with 2629 patients, surgery was associated with a higher remission rate than medical therapy (67% vs. 45%), although studies were noncomparative and had high heterogeneity and imprecision. As noted above, primary surgical remission rates decrease with duration of follow-up; in one study, only 51% remained in primary surgical remission at a mean follow-up of 100 months.

In one cohort study of long-term follow-up in 266 patients with acromegaly, 93.2% achieved a normal IGF-1 level during 9.9 (5.0-15.0) years follow-up with multimodality therapy. The interval to first normal IGF-1 level following failed surgical remission prior to 2006 was 27.5 (95% CI, 22.0-36.0) months and significantly shorter after 2006 at 14.0 (95% CI, 10.0-20.0) months likely due to increased use of radiation therapy and reoperation.

Based on recommendations from the Acromegaly Consensus Group and the Endocine Society guidelines, optimal disease control is IGF-I level in the age-adjusted normal range determined by a reliable standard assay and GH level <1 mcg/L from a random GH measurement or nadir GH after an oral glucose tolerance test of <0.4 mcg/L.

AACE recommends obtaining a GH value at 1 week postoperatively using a nadir as above to define initial disease control. A reassessment of biochemical activity at 3 and 6 months after surgery is considered a more valid determination of surgical efficacy. The Endocrine Society guidelines suggests measuring IGF-1 and a random GH level at 12 weeks or later following surgery along with an imaging study at least 12 weeks after surgery to visualize residual tumor and adjacent structures.

In an observational cohort study, following transsphenoidal adenomectomy, remission was seen in 157 of 187 patients with acromegaly and there was no difference in metabolic parameters at 1 year between the 136 patients achieving nadir GH of 0.4 ng/mL and the 21 patients achieving a nadir GH of 1.0 ng/mL.

Postoperatively, posterior pituitary and adrenal, thyroid, and gonadal function should be monitored, the former at approximately 2 weeks. Hyponatremia due to the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of anti-diuretic hormone occurs at postoperative days 5 to 14 in 5% to 10% of patients and transient diabetes insipidus in about 20% after transsphenoidal surgery. Thyroid and gonadal function should be reevaluated 6 to 12 weeks postoperatively.

Patients require monitoring of IGF/GH at least every 6 months and MRI imaging of the pituitary at least yearly, as well as surveillance for the complications associated with acromegaly, such as diabetes, cardiomyopathy, sleep apnea, and colon polyps.
IGF-1 levels are also recommended annually in all patients postoperatively, as recurrences can occur up to 20 years later.

In one retrospective study of 463 patients with acromegaly, surgical remission rates were higher for men than women (89.7% and 76.5%, respectively), with women having larger and more aggressive tumors.
For patients undergoing radiotherapy, the Endocrine Society guidelines suggest annual hormonal testing for hypopituitarism and other delayed radiation effects.

Symptoms can be measured using the Patient Assessed Acromegaly Symptom Questionnaire, although this questionnaire has not been validated. Authors of a meta-analysis of 24 papers found reduced symptoms following treatment with a decrease in total symptom score of –2.3 points (95% CI –1.3 to –3.3 points). Individual symptom score decreases were: –0.9 (95% CI, –0.6 to –1.2) for paresthesia, –0.4 (95% CI, –0.1 to –0.6) for hyperhidrosis, –0.3 (95% CI, –0.1 to –0.6) for fatigue, –0.3 (95% CI, –0.1 to –0.5) for arthralgia, –0.3 (95% CI, 0.0 to –0.6) for headache, and –0.2 (95% CI, 0.0 to –0.4) for soft-tissue swelling.

The Acromegaly Quality of Life Questionnaire can be used to monitor this important aspect of health, although this questionnaire has also not been validated. The tool is a self-rating questionnaire consisting of 22 items covering physical (8 items) and a psychological (14 items, divided equally over the 2 subscales appearance and personal relations) factors contributing to patient quality of life. Scores range from 22 (worst) to 110 (best).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 22 studies on acromegaly that included health-related-quality of life measured by the above instrument found improvement in 12 studies (55%), with similar before and after treatment ratings in the remaining studies. Overall, quality of life improved by 2.9 points (95% CI 0.5 to 5.3 points).
The Acromegaly Consensus Group (2020) recommend measurement of blood pressure every 6 months and an annual electrocardiogram and echocardiography if the initial tests are abnormal.

Patients can be evaluated for OSA through use of the Epworth Sleepiness Scale or a sleep study if sleep apnea is suspected. In a study of 27 consecutive patients with treatment-naive acromegaly, sleep apnea was diagnosed in 74.1%. After 2.5 years of treatment, all patients had controlled acromegaly and 11 (68.8%) were cured of OSA.

For women with menstrual dysfunction or when pregnancy is desired, the Acromegaly Consensus Guideline recommends obtaining LH, FSH, 17 ß-estradiol, and prolactin annually to assess for hypogonadism and hyperprolactinemia.

For men with active acromegaly, the Acromegaly Consensus guideline recommends measuring total testosterone, sex hormone binding globulin, and prolactin annually. Obtain free testosterone levels if the test results are unclear to avoid overdiagnosis of hypogonadism.

For patients on SRLs, routine monitoring for gallbladder disease with abdominal ultrasound should be considered. For patients on pegvisomant, consider liver function testing monthly for 6 months, then every 6 months and serial imaging with MRI to evaluate tumor size.

Most women with acromegaly during pregnancy do not experience an increase in tumor size or metabolic complications. Neonatal outcomes also appear unaffected, although fetal weight change (both micro- and macrosomia) may occur depending on needed treatment. SRLs, dopamine agonists, and the GH-receptor agonist have been reported as safe during pregnancy, based on case series.

Authors of a meta-analysis 19 studies including 273 pregnancies in 211 women with acromegaly found an overall frequency of control of acromegaly during pregnancy of 62%, and tumor growth occurred in 9%. No fetal or maternal deaths were reported. Development of gestational diabetes was 9%, premature labor occurred in 9% (95% CI 5-13%); spontaneous miscarriage in 4% (95% CI 2-11%), small for gestational age in 5% (95% CI 3-9%), and congenital malformations occurred in 1% (95% CI 0-7%).

The Endocrine Society guideline suggests discontinuing long-acting SRL formulations and pegvisomant about 2 months prior to attempted conception in favor of short-acting octreotide until conception. After conception, medical therapy should be administered only for tumor or headache control.
Biochemical monitoring with GH or IGF-1 is of limited use in pregnancy.
Serial visual field testing can be conducted in pregnant women with macroadenomas.
